clue.text: Broken arm having mended, do some knitting?

definitions.meaning: once a fractured limb has healed, the plaster that held it is removed
a knitter finishes work by securing the last stitches and taking them off the needle

explanation.surface: Someone whose fractured arm has healed celebrates by picking up the knitting needles again.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is a description rather than a dictionary definition: a healed arm has its plaster cast taken off. The question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one phrase: removing plaster from a healed limb, and the knitting term for finishing off stitches.

clue.text: Vehicle advanced on iron vessel

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: A car pulls up beside an iron ship or container.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass flask for serving wine or water is a kind of vessel, a container for liquid.

clue.text: Singular approach of primate-catcher?

parts.note: the old saying '..., ..., catchee monkey' gives the method twice; said once, singly, it is one word

explanation.surface: A question about how someone sets out to catch a monkey.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'softly, softly, catchee monkey' urges patience; 'Singular' asks for just one of its two repeated words.
explanation.definitionFit: Gently and quietly is how the proverb says a monkey is caught, so the adverb names that approach.

clue.text: Was of greater importance, so able to walk better through water, they say

indicators.note: signals that the letters entered are a word that sounds like the phrase before it

parts.words: able to walk better through water
parts.note: to out-wade someone is to wade further or better than they can; 'so able' gives the past form out-waded

explanation.surface: Something mattered more, so a person could stride better through water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'they say' gives a word that sounds like OUT-WADED, past tense of out-wade, to beat at wading.
explanation.definitionFit: To be heavier or more significant than something else, in the past tense, is to have been of greater importance.

clue.text: Flash unfashionable attire — reduced!

indicators.note: the attire word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: flares, wide-bottomed trousers, are widely seen as dated

explanation.surface: A shop flashes a sale sign: out-of-date clothes, marked down!
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' takes the last letter off FLARES, the bell-bottomed trousers of the 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden burst of light, like one fired from a distress gun, is a flash.

clue.text: Protect offspring of hound by taking son inside

indicators.note: the pieces from 'by taking son' go within the word for hound

parts.note: to bait someone is to harass or hound them
taken as written

explanation.surface: A parent protects a puppy from a hunting dog by bringing a boy indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hound' is a verb meaning harass, not a dog. 'taking' adds S to BY, and 'inside' puts the result in the middle of the hound word.
explanation.definitionFit: To mind children while the parents are out is to look after and protect someone else's young.

clue.text: Prominent features of 'dandy champers'

parts.note: a buck is an old word for a fashionable young man, a dandy
teeth are what champ, or chew noisily, so they are champers

explanation.surface: A fancy-dress dandy's notable trait: his big front teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'champers' looks like slang for champagne; here it means things that champ.
explanation.definitionFit: Protruding upper front teeth stick out, making them prominent features of a face.

clue.text: Blair's reported prosperity

definitions.meaning: the name Blair sounds like blare, a loud deep noise such as a cannon's roar
a period of rapid economic growth

explanation.surface: News coverage claims Tony Blair's era was one of prosperity.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Blair was UK Prime Minister 1997-2007. Spoken, 'Blair's' is 'blares', and to blare is to make a deep resonant noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud resonant noise, and also a period of sudden economic growth: two senses of one word.

clue.text: Revolutionary scientific facility — Pascal be damned!

indicators.note: something damned is wrecked or ruined, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A scientist curses Pascal while at a groundbreaking research centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests groundbreaking; here it means orbiting the Earth.
explanation.definitionFit: A laboratory carried in orbit revolves round the Earth, making it a scientific facility that literally revolves.

clue.text: Northern area supports, of course, sports team

parts.note: on a golf course, tees are the pegs that support balls
a side is a team in sport

explanation.surface: A northern region naturally backs its local team.
explanation.walkthrough: TEESSIDE is the area around the River Tees in north-east England, including Middlesbrough. 'of course' seems to mean 'naturally' but points to a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: The region around the River Tees lies in the north-east of England, so it is a northern area.

clue.text: Makeover: about to get sexually desirable

parts.note: re means about or concerning
fit is British slang for attractive

explanation.surface: A makeover is about to make someone look sexy.
explanation.walkthrough: FIT meaning attractive is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A renovation or refurbishment, especially of a ship or building, is a makeover.

clue.text: US city gets a new church — with nothing to go up the wall

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing
to go up the wall is to become furious, to rage

explanation.surface: An American city builds a new church with no plan for climbing its walls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go up the wall' sounds like climbing; it is the idiom for losing your temper.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest city in Alaska is a US city.

clue.text: Fine-tuned athletes, packed with energy, taken out at night?

indicators.note: the energy letter is stuffed into the middle of the other letters

parts.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

indicators.note: to tune is to adjust, so these letters are adjusted into a new order

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Finely honed sportsmen, full of energy, go out on the town at night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tuned' rearranges ATHLETES to ALSETETH; 'packed with' puts E inside, after F. 'Fine-tuned' looks like one word but splits into F and the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Dentures are often removed before bed, a cryptic hint at something taken out of the mouth overnight.

clue.text: See 21
Qualified, reportedly, to identify island's salt

parts.note: able means capable or qualified

indicators.note: signals that the following letters sound like the phrase spoken

parts.note: to see is to identify, and the Isle of Man is the island, so see Man

explanation.surface: A competent chemist, as rumoured, identifies an island's salt.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea. 'salt' looks chemical but means an old sailor; an able seaman is a naval rank.
explanation.definitionFit: An old salt is an experienced sailor, and an able seaman is a trained sailor.

clue.text: Get too enthusiastic and hit the drink

definitions.meaning: to do something to excess, getting carried away
to fall off a ship into the sea, the drink being slang for water

explanation.surface: Someone overexcited starts drinking heavily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit the drink' sounds like boozing; the drink is slang for the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one phrase: overdoing something in excess, and falling from a vessel into the water.

clue.text: Gay choir formed around end of April, a powerful group

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go round the last letter picked
the choir's letters are formed into a new arrangement
the final letter of April is the one taken

explanation.surface: A gay choir assembles in late April as an influential body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'formed' rearranges GAY CHOIR; 'around' wraps those letters round L, from 'end of April'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rule by a small elite, or the elite itself, is a powerful group.

clue.text: Unknown number longing to include time out on the water?

parts.note: Y is an algebraic unknown

indicators.note: the time letter is taken into the middle of the other letters

parts.note: aching means yearning or longing

explanation.surface: An unknown number of people long to take time out on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'time out' looks like a phrase, but 'time' gives T and 'out on the water' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailing in a sailing boat for pleasure is an activity spent out on the water.

clue.text: Finger twisted inside hollowed-out Kenyan rainforest plant

indicators.note: the shuffled letters go between the two letters left
with its middle removed, only the first and last letters of the word remain
the word's letters are twisted out of order

explanation.surface: A finger gets caught in a hollow inside a Kenyan forest plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hollowed-out' leaves just the first and last letters of Kenyan; 'twisted' shuffles Finger, and 'inside' puts the shuffle between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A large tropical fern found in rainforests is a rainforest plant.

clue.text: A tender baritone finally accompanying Brummie hymn

parts.note: to tender is to offer, as is a bid

indicators.note: the last letter of baritone is the one taken

parts.note: with means accompanying
the setter's pseudonym, so the setter is me

explanation.surface: A gentle baritone at last joins Brummie singing a hymn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tender' looks like gentle; it is the noun offer. Setters refer to themselves by name, so Brummie gives ME.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian hymn by Henry Lyte, sung at funerals and the FA Cup final, is a well-known hymn.

clue.text: Coalition: the French disease

parts.note: le is French for the
ague is an old word for a fever such as malaria

explanation.surface: A political alliance is dismissed as the French sickness.
explanation.definitionFit: An alliance of groups united for a purpose is a coalition.

clue.text: Narrow part said to be in line

indicators.note: signals that the letters entered sound like a word for in line

parts.note: straight means aligned, in line

explanation.surface: A narrow section is claimed to be properly aligned.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow channel of water joining two seas is a narrow part.

clue.text: Notes broadcast far from land?

indicators.note: signals that the letters entered sound like the notes spoken

parts.note: top Cs are ... notes, ... Cs

explanation.surface: Musical notes are broadcast from a ship far out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' looks like a radio transmission; it signals the sound of HIGH Cs.
explanation.definitionFit: Open ocean beyond any country's coastal waters is far from land.

clue.text: Confusion when two females replace centre of gutter in parapet

indicators.note: the female letters take the place of letters from the middle

parts.note: a battlement is a parapet with gaps along a castle wall

indicators.note: the middle two letters of gutter are the ones taken

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for female, so two give FF

explanation.surface: Confusion reigns as two women repair a gutter in a parapet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre of gutter' is TT; 'replace' swaps it in BATTLEMENT for FF.
explanation.definitionFit: Being puzzled or perplexed is a state of confusion.

clue.text: Cut line by knot's end

parts.note: a file is a line, as in single file

indicators.note: the last letter of knot is the one taken

explanation.surface: Slice a rope beside where the knot finishes.
explanation.definitionFit: A boneless slice of meat or fish is a cut, the French spelling of fillet.

clue.text: Away with this illicit cruiser!

parts.note: the answer word joined with 'away' makes a hidden passenger who travels without paying

explanation.surface: An order to get rid of an illegal boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Away with this' sounds like 'get rid of it'; it means 'this word plus AWAY', giving a stowaway, an illicit cruiser.
explanation.definitionFit: Hidden aboard without a ticket, a stowaway takes a cruise illicitly; the answer completes that word.

clue.text: Description of certain pod members rendered in dialect

indicators.note: to render is to recast, so these letters are recast in a new order

explanation.surface: A description of some whales in a pod is given in local dialect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pod members' suggests whales or dolphins; it means peas, alike as two peas in a pod.
explanation.definitionFit: Peas in one pod are proverbially exactly alike, so this adjective describes them.

clue.text: Molten material's reduced periodical state

indicators.note: the periodical word is cut short to its common short form

parts.note: a magazine is a periodical
MA is the postal abbreviation for Massachusetts

explanation.surface: A cut-down magazine reports on the state of molten rock.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot liquid rock beneath the Earth's crust is molten material.

clue.text: Passage from Burns' Go With Style

parts.note: gang is Scots for go, as used by the poet Robert Burns
a way of doing something is its style

explanation.surface: A route to follow taken from the poems of Burns, Go With Style.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns wrote in Scots; 'gang aft agley' in 'To a Mouse' uses gang for go.
explanation.definitionFit: A path between rows of seats or onto a ship is a passage.

clue.text: A touching feature of Dynasty (Net version)

parts.note: the Tang were a Chinese imperial dynasty

indicators.note: a new version is a reworking, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A moving scene from the TV soap Dynasty, in an online version.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touching' looks emotional; in geometry a straight line that touches a curve at one point is a tangent.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry this line meets a curve at a single point without crossing it, a feature that touches.
